title: Apple and Alphabet are sending Wall Street different signals
detail:
Apple and Alphabet are sending Wall Street different signals
Hillary Remy, Dana Sullivan Kilroy
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 9:47 AM MST 5 min read
AAPL
GOOG
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The two biggest AI bets on Wall Street are not making the same one. One company is writing checks that would strain most national budgets. The other is letting partners do the heavy lifting while it sells the hardware everyone else needs.

Retirement savers feel that split most. A portfolio that is meant to last decades has different needs than a trade meant to pay off next quarter, and the debate comes down to Alphabet versus Apple. Both report earnings this month, so the timing is hard to ignore.

How the Alphabet and Apple gap opened up

Alphabet has lost about $860 billion in market value since its peak, close to Walmart's $937.1 billion, according to 24/7 Wall St., citing an October 17 post by Charlie Bilello of Creative Planning that put Apple at an all-time high and Alphabet 17% below.

Apple is worth $4.95 trillion and Alphabet is worth $4.21 trillion. Apple leads the Magnificent Seven this year at 25.26%, against 6.47% for Alphabet, which has also fallen 4.84% in the past month.

Also read: Apple just made a surprising move with a popular product

Apple's run is real. The stock touched an all-time high of $345.34 in September, weeks after John Ternus became CEO on September 1, and was up 25% for the year with a market value just under $5 trillion, according to TheStreet. The iPhone 18 lineup went on sale September 19 with prices raised by $100, and the $1,999 foldable iPhone Duo ships October 23.

Alphabet went the other way after July's earnings. Revenue beat estimates and Google Cloud grew 82% to $24.8 billion, but the company lifted its 2026 capex outlook to $195 billion to $205 billion, up from $180 billion to $190 billion, and the stock sank.

The next test arrives on October 28. Alphabet brought in $119.8 billion in second-quarter sales, up 24%, yet Bank of America expects about $199 billion of capex this year and $301 billion in 2027, plus a $12.4 billion free cash flow loss in the third quarter. The bank also expects Search growth to cool from 17% to 14% while Cloud accelerates to 93%.

What Alphabet's spending is doing to its cash

Alphabet spent $44.9 billion on capital expenditures in the second quarter, double the year-earlier amount, and posted its first negative free cash flow since going public in 2004, according to Axios, citing FactSet. Net income got a lift from roughly $99 billion in net gains on equity securities.

Alphabet was the first hyperscaler to report this season, Axios noted, so investors read its spending as a signal for the group.

To pay for the buildout, Alphabet announced plans to raise $80 billion in equity in June, including a $10 billion private placement to Berkshire Hathaway at $351.81 per Class A share and $348.20 per Class C share, Bloomberg reported. The company said demand for its AI services exceeds the supply it can deliver.

title: Is Kroger Stock Increasing Your Market Risk?

Is Kroger Stock Increasing Your Market Risk?

If you own Kroger (KR), or are weighing the stock after its 8.2% rise in the five sessions to October 22, 2026, your position most likely sits alongside capital tracking the S&P 500. Every day the index fluctuates, Kroger's performance blends with the rest of those holdings. So does Kroger add to the risk you already carry, or work against it?

Kroger Stock Has Moved Against The Market

Over the past year, from October 21, 2025, to October 22, 2026, Kroger shares moved against the broader market. A $10,000 holding in Kroger fell about $35 on an average day the S&P 500 rose, and gained about $43 on an average day the index declined. For each 1% the S&P 500 moved over the past year, Kroger tended to shift about 0.71% the other way.

That dynamic does not make Kroger a calm stock. Its volatility, the typical size of its swings over a year, was 29.8%, more than double the S&P 500's 12.7%. While Kroger steadied a broader market portfolio over the past year, the shares brought larger swings of their own.

Will Kroger Keep Moving Like This?

Kroger is reshaping its operations during a period of slow sales growth, which gives investors more to weigh. In September 2026, management lowered its full-year forecast for identical sales without fuel, its measure of sales growth at existing stores, to 0.5% at the midpoint from 1.5%. The company maintained its full-year profit forecast.

Kroger laid out a multi-year plan on October 20, 2026, introducing new long-term targets that run through 2029. Management expects its planned acquisition of Giant Eagle to close in 2027. Separately, Albertsons is seeking $8 billion from Kroger over their failed merger, with a trial looming, news reports said on October 12, 2026.

The direction of Kroger's moves is less settled than their size. From October 2021 to October 2026, the stock's daily moves showed almost no connection to the index, posting a correlation of 0.05, where zero means no link. Moving against the broader market is a recent pattern for Kroger, while its wide swings have persisted longer.

Has Kroger Stock Paid You For Its Swings?

Over the five years from October 23, 2021, to October 22, 2026, Kroger paid you slightly more than the market, but yielded less for each unit of swing. The stock returned 13.5% a year during that window, compared with 12.6% for the S&P 500. Kroger posted an annual volatility of 27.4%, against 17.0% for the index.

Dividing the return by the volatility reveals how much each unit of swing earned: 0.493 for Kroger and 0.741 for the S&P 500. A higher figure means the swings paid better, so the market rewarded you more for each unit of swing.

title: What Could Go Wrong With Amazon Stock?
detail:
What Could Go Wrong With Amazon Stock?
Trefis Team
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 1:00 AM MST 3 min read

GOOG
WMT
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Amazon.com (AMZN) earned $135 billion in net income over the four quarters ended June 2026, well above its $93.7 billion of operating income. Yet its free cash flow, the cash left after paying for new buildings and equipment, was a negative $11.6 billion over the same twelve months. That gap is the number a holder should watch, because a company spending more cash than it brings in has to cover the difference somewhere. So where is all that cash going?

Amazon Is Spending Its Cash On AI Data Centers

Most of it is funding new capacity for AWS, Amazon's cloud business, and for generative AI. During the June quarter alone, Amazon spent $53.1 billion in cash on capital projects, compared with the $45.4 billion in cash its operations brought in. Management said this spending supports strong customer demand. Even at its planned spending for the year, management said Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all the demand it sees in 2026. Management believes the same will be true in 2027.

The bill is also growing. Management now expects about $220 billion of cash capital spending in 2026, up from its earlier estimate of about $200 billion, because memory costs more.

How Fast Has Amazon's Free Cash Flow Fallen?

Amazon's free cash flow has fallen in each of the last two twelve-month periods. The figure stood at $48.3 billion in the twelve months from July 2023 to June 2024, dropped to $13.5 billion from July 2024 to June 2025, and then turned negative in the latest twelve months.

Debt has climbed over the same stretch. Amazon's total debt reached $223 billion at the end of June 2026, up from $134 billion a year earlier. Management also said on its July 30, 2026 call that the company has issued debt in 2026.

The wait for a return is long, too. Management said Amazon begins spending data center money two years before it can put servers into the buildings and start earning from them. So some of the money Amazon spends today will not earn anything for a while.

What Are Amazon Investors Paying For Now?

Investors pay 19.9 times Amazon's earnings, against 23.0 for the S&P 500. That multiple looks low partly because Amazon's net income, lifted by items outside its main operations, sits well above its operating income. Measured against operating income, investors pay about 28.8 times.

The best case against the worry is that much of the demand is already signed. Management said Amazon's backlog stood at $496 billion on the July call, growing at a triple-digit rate from a year earlier. AWS revenue grew 36.7% from a year earlier in the June quarter. Management also said servers and networking equipment take a little less than three years to break even, while most of its AI capacity is contracted for at least five-year terms. Because Amazon buys servers only a few months before putting them to use, it will not spend that money if the demand is not there, management added.

The S&P 500 has always been an index offering a clear picture of the companies driving the U.S. economy, and in its earlier days, energy and manufacturing companies found themselves at the top. But this picture rapidly changed over the past decade as technology players gained momentum in earnings growth and stock performance.

A company's position leading the famous index depends on its market capitalization, and it also must be primarily owned by the public, rather than by founders, for example. Today, this puts three tech giants in the top spot -- and they are followed by several other tech powerhouses. In fact, we only start seeing companies from other industries around the 10th position. At this point, companies including Eli Lilly, Berkshire Hathaway, and Walmart broaden the index's exposure into other industries.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Considering all of this, the S&P 500 may depend on the fortunes of the following three companies right now. Let's consider the good news and the bad news for investors.

Image source: Getty Images.

A transition at the top of the S&P 500

So, first, let's consider how this transition from energy, manufacturing, and even consumer-related companies to tech stocks dominating the S&P 500 took place. As mentioned, the index is a reflection of the businesses leading the economy, and the fast growth of tech companies, from Internet and e-commerce players to chip designers and cloud service providers, catapulted them into the driver's seat.

The last time a non-tech player was in the top three of the S&P 500 was back in 2014, and that was ExxonMobil, according to FinHacker data. The energy company was No. 2 after Apple, and these top companies' market values were in the hundreds of billions of dollars -- not in the trillions as leading S&P 500 companies are today.

As tech companies' earnings soared, investors piled in, market cap advanced, and the rest is history. This brings us to the subject of today's biggest S&P 500 companies, and they are Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft, with weightings of about 8%, 7%, and 5%, respectively. That means that, together, they carry a weight of about 20%. Considering that fellow tech giants follow in the top 10 positions, the S&P 500 depends heavily on the fortunes of tech companies today, particularly Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft.

title: Kimberly-Clark vs. Coca-Cola: Which Dividend Stock Is the Better Buy Now?
detail:
Kimberly-Clark vs. Coca-Cola: Which Dividend Stock Is the Better Buy Now?
Jack Delaney, The Motley Fool
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 6:15 PM MST 5 min read
KMB
KO
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors often turn to defensive sectors when looking for stability during market shifts. Kimberly-Clark (NASDAQ:KMB) and Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO) represent two iconic choices for those seeking reliable businesses with deep global roots.

Kimberly-Clark focuses on hygiene and personal care essentials that consumers buy regardless of economic conditions. Coca-Cola dominates the global beverage landscape with a focus on brand power and high profitability. This comparison examines which stock provides a more compelling balance of growth and value today.

The case for Kimberly-Clark

Kimberly-Clark operates as a global leader in personal care and hygiene, manufacturing essential products like Huggies diapers and Kleenex tissues. The company sells these items to a wide range of retail partners, including supermarkets, drugstores, and e-commerce platforms. Its largest customer is Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT), which accounted for approximately 16% of net sales in 2025. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $16.4 billion, representing a decrease of approximately 2.1% compared to the prior year. This revenue decline was accompanied by net income of roughly $2 billion. Despite the top-line pressure, the company showed its ability to generate profit from its consumer staples stocks portfolio.

The case for Coca-Cola

Coca-Cola is the world's largest non-alcoholic beverage company, owning brands ranging from its flagship soda to sports drinks and coffee. The company relies on a network of independent bottling partners to package and distribute its products. Starting in 2027, the company will expand its reach by replacing PepsiCo (NASDAQ:PEP) at all U.S. KFC restaurants.

In FY 2025, revenue grew by nearly 1.9% to reach approximately $47.9 billion. This growth helped the company achieve a net income of roughly $13.1 billion for the fiscal period. Coca-Cola recorded a net margin of approximately 27.3%, which highlights the strength of its global branding and licensing business model.

Risk profile comparison

Kimberly-Clark faces risks regarding the integration of its pending acquisition of Kenvue (NYSE:KVUE), which could impact financial flexibility. The company also deals with intense competition from private-label manufacturers and the rising bargaining power of large retailers. Supply chain vulnerabilities are another concern, as price volatility for materials like cellulose fiber and petroleum can erode net margins. Geopolitical instability also threatens international revenue and supply lines.
